title: PowerShell
summary: PowerShell is a scripting language and functional command-line shell built on .NET, used throughout enterprise networks to automate updates, software management, and security tasks at both the server and client level. Every cmdlet follows a strict Verb-Noun naming pattern, everything a cmdlet returns is an object with inspectable properties and methods, and cmdlets chain together through the pipeline (|). Cyber operators lean on this constantly — for enumeration, automation, and remote administration over WinRM.

commands.description: Displays the PowerShell host's version — the quickest way to check whether you're in Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7.x.
Switches the current session into PowerShell 7.x (Core) from Windows PowerShell 5.1. Both versions are installed side by side on modern Windows.
Closes the current PowerShell session and returns to whatever session launched it — the way back from pwsh to 5.1.
Displays help for a cmdlet. -Online opens the Microsoft docs page in a browser; -Full or -Detailed adds parameter descriptions and examples.
Displays an about_ conceptual topic explaining PowerShell's help syntax notation: [-Name] means optional/positional, <type> means a required value.
Lists the cmdlets, functions, and aliases available in the current session. Can be filtered with -Type, -Module, or -Noun.
Shows which cmdlet an alias actually maps to — dir resolves to Get-ChildItem.
Lists every property and method available on the object(s) a cmdlet returns, along with the object's TypeName.
Projects only the named properties from each object in the pipeline, dropping everything else.
Filters piped objects using a script block; $_ represents the current object flowing through the pipeline.
The shorthand Where-Object syntax — -Property -Operator Value — returns the exact same result as the script-block form.
Launches a process, using the .NET Process.Start() method under the hood.
Terminates a running process by name, using the .NET Process.Kill() method under the hood.
Controls how returned objects are displayed — as a compact table (ft) or a one-property-per-line list (fl).
Creates a new file (or -Type Directory for a folder) at the given path.
Deletes an item. -Verbose confirms what happened; -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue hides errors if the item doesn't exist.
Shows the script execution policy for every scope (Machine, User, Process, etc). The default is Restricted.
Changes the script execution policy for a given scope — required before most .ps1 scripts will run.
Queries a CIM class for management data — the modern, faster replacement for the deprecated Get-WmiObject.
Creates the current user's PowerShell profile script, since profiles don't exist by default.
Enables PowerShell Remoting on a client OS. The flag is required when a Public network profile is active, and adds a firewall rule limited to the local subnet.
Runs a script block on a remote computer over WinRM and returns the results — a one-to-one temporary remoting session.
Adds a host to the client's TrustedHosts list, required for WinRM to use NTLM auth outside an Active Directory domain.

terms.description: A native PowerShell command using strict Verb-Noun naming, e.g. Get-Process — nouns are always singular (Get-Process, never Get-Processes).
Passes the output object(s) of one cmdlet as input to the next cmdlet using the | operator, letting commands be chained together.
Represents the current object flowing through the pipeline inside a script block, e.g. {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"}. Always the same type as the object from the previous command.
Everything a PowerShell cmdlet returns is an object with properties (data) and methods (actions) — Get-Member reveals both, plus the object's TypeName.
The protocol PowerShell Remoting uses instead of the older DCOM, built on WS-Management; needs only one firewall port and encrypts traffic with a per-session AES-256 key.
The SOAP-based device-management protocol that WinRM implements, letting PowerShell Remoting simplify network configuration to a single open port.
A vendor-neutral object model for describing management data (hardware, OS, services); WMI classes are built directly on top of CIM classes.
Microsoft's implementation of CIM, used to query and manage Windows subsystems like the BIOS, disks, and processes; Get-CimInstance is its modern successor cmdlet.
Controls whether, and which, PowerShell scripts (.ps1 files) are allowed to run on a system; defaults to Restricted, which blocks nearly everything.
A .ps1 script (not created by default) that runs automatically whenever a matching PowerShell session starts, used to persist aliases, functions, and settings.
A variable PowerShell creates and maintains on its own, e.g. $_, $?, $PSVersionTable, $PROFILE, $HOME, and $ERROR — never assigned by the user.
A short alternate name that maps to a cmdlet, e.g. dir -> Get-ChildItem; aliases you create yourself are lost when the session closes unless saved in a profile.
A client-side list of hosts that PowerShell Remoting will trust for NTLM authentication outside an Active Directory domain, where Kerberos isn't available.
A recorded log of everything typed and returned in a PowerShell session, started with Start-Transcript and ended with Stop-Transcript. Doesn't work inside the ISE.
The older Windows remote-object technology that PowerShell Remoting (via WinRM) was built to replace, requiring more firewall ports and offering weaker encryption.

facts: PowerShell cmdlets follow a strict Verb-Noun naming pattern with a singular noun, e.g. Get-Process, never Get-Processes.
Parameters begin with a dash (-Name) unless they are positional; Get-Service -Name bits and Get-Service bits are functionally identical.
PowerShell 1.0 through 5.1 run on the .NET Framework and are Windows-only; PowerShell Core (pwsh) runs on .NET Core and is cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux).
Windows 10 ships with PowerShell 5.1 by default. Typing pwsh switches into PowerShell 7.x side by side; exit returns to the previous session's version.
Everything a PowerShell cmdlet returns is an object — Get-Member reveals its TypeName plus every property and method available on it.
$_ inside a Where-Object script block always refers to the current object flowing through the pipeline, and is always the same type as the object from the previous command.
Get-Help searches both a cmdlet's own help page and its related about_ conceptual topic at the same time; individual about_ topics can also be searched directly, e.g. Get-Help about_command_syntax.
The default PowerShell script Execution Policy is Restricted, which blocks all scripts not created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup.
PowerShell Remoting (available since PowerShell v2) uses WinRM/WS-Management instead of DCOM, needing only one open firewall port, with traffic encrypted by a per-session AES-256 key.

WinRM defaults to Kerberos authentication on port 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS, requires a certificate). Outside an Active Directory domain, a host must be added to TrustedHosts, or HTTPS must be used instead.
Connecting to a remote session by IP address instead of hostname prevents Kerberos from being used — NTLM authentication is used instead, which requires the target to be listed in TrustedHosts.
PowerShell profiles are plain .ps1 scripts and are not created by default; custom aliases and variables set interactively are lost when the session closes unless they're saved to a profile.

Setting WSMan TrustedHosts to "*" trusts every possible host and overrides one of the strongest built-in protections against spoofed connections and credential theft — acceptable for throwaway testing only, never production.
CIM classes are the vendor-neutral parent model that Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) classes are built on; Get-CimInstance is the modern, faster replacement for the deprecated Get-WmiObject.

Enabling PowerShell Remoting on a client OS with an active Public network profile requires the -SkipNetworkProfileCheck flag on Enable-PSRemoting, which adds a firewall rule limited to hosts on the local subnet.

questions.questionHtml: Which naming convention do all PowerShell cmdlets follow?

options.html: Verb-Noun, with the noun always singular (e.g. Get-Process)
Noun-Verb, with the noun always plural (e.g. Process-Get)
camelCase function names with no hyphen
snake_case command names

questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell cmdlets always use Verb-Noun syntax, and the noun is always singular — Get-Process, never Get-Processes.

questions.questionHtml: You write a PowerShell script against one PowerShell version, then run it against a target running a different version. What should you expect?

options.html: Nothing — scripts are always fully version-independent
A high likelihood of the script failing or producing errors
The script automatically upgrades itself to match the target
PowerShell refuses to load any cross-version script file

questions.explanationHtml: Because functionality and even syntax can differ between versions, a script written for one PowerShell version has a high likelihood of failing or erroring when run against a different version. Always be mindful of the version in use.

questions.questionHtml: Which command switches the current console session from Windows PowerShell 5.1 into PowerShell 7.x?

options.html: switch-ps
pwsh
powershell -v7
Update-PowerShell

questions.explanationHtml: Typing pwsh at the prompt drops you into PowerShell 7.x, since both versions are installed side by side on modern Windows.

questions.questionHtml: After typing pwsh to move from PowerShell 5.1 into 7.3, how do you return to the previous 5.1 session?

options.html: exit
pwsh -exit
Stop-Session
Close-PSSession

questions.explanationHtml: exit closes the current session and drops you back into whichever session launched it — from 7.3 back to 5.1.

questions.questionHtml: Which two statements about PowerShell parameters are correct? (Choose two.)

options.html: Parameters always begin with a dash unless they are positional
PowerShell uses spaces as parameter delimiters
Every parameter must always include a leading dash, with no exceptions
A parameter value containing spaces can never be passed, even in quotes

questions.explanationHtml: Parameters begin with a dash unless they're positional (no dash required), and PowerShell separates parameters with spaces. A value containing spaces just needs to be wrapped in quotes, e.g. Get-Content -Path "C:\Test Files\content.txt".

questions.questionHtml: Get-Service -Name bits is functionally identical to which other command?

options.html: Get-Service Name bits
Get-Service bits
Get-Service -bits
Find-Service bits

questions.explanationHtml: -Name is a positional parameter, so the dash-and-name can be dropped entirely: Get-Service bits means the same thing.

questions.questionHtml: What does running Get-Process | Get-Member show you?

options.html: Only the running process names
The object's TypeName plus every property and method available on it
Live, continuously-updating memory usage
Whether each process binary is digitally signed

questions.explanationHtml: Get-Member returns the TypeName of the piped object (e.g. System.Diagnostics.Process) along with every property and method it exposes.

options.html: Every service on the system, regardless of status
The current object flowing through the pipeline from the previous command
A variable the user must manually declare beforehand
The literal text "Status"

questions.explanationHtml: $_ is the pipelined variable — it represents whichever object is currently passing through the pipeline, and is always the same type as the object produced by the previous command.

questions.questionHtml: How do the results of Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"} and Get-Service | where Status -eq "Stopped" compare?

options.html: They return the exact same result — one is just shorthand for the other
Only the script-block form is valid PowerShell syntax
The shorthand form requires piping through Format-Table first to work
"where" is not a recognized alias for Where-Object

questions.explanationHtml: Both are Where-Object — the second just uses the shorthand -Property -Operator Value form and the where alias instead of the full script-block syntax. The results are identical.

questions.questionHtml: What is the default PowerShell script Execution Policy on a fresh Windows installation?

options.html: Unrestricted
Bypass
Restricted
AllSigned

questions.explanationHtml: The default policy is Restricted, which disallows all scripts that weren't created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup — a deliberate security default, since scripts can carry malicious code.

questions.questionHtml: Which technology does PowerShell Remoting use instead of the older DCOM?

options.html: RDP
WinRM, built on WS-Management
SMB Direct
SSH exclusively

questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell Remoting (available since PowerShell v2) uses WinRM, which implements WS-Management — simplifying network configuration to one firewall port and encrypting all traffic.

questions.questionHtml: By default, which port does WinRM use for unencrypted HTTP traffic?
questions.explanationHtml: WinRM defaults to port 5985 for HTTP. Port 5986 is used for HTTPS, which requires additional certificate setup.

questions.questionHtml: You attempt PowerShell Remoting to a workgroup (non-domain) computer using its IP address instead of hostname. What happens?

options.html: Kerberos can't be used with an IP address, so NTLM auth is used instead — requiring the target to be listed in TrustedHosts
PowerShell Remoting refuses all IP-address connections outright
Only HTTPS connections are ever permitted to workgroup computers
WinRM automatically falls back to using DCOM

questions.explanationHtml: New-PSSession, Enter-PSSession, and Invoke-Command all accept an IP address, but Kerberos does not work with one — NTLM authentication is used instead, which means the target host must be added to the client's TrustedHosts list (or HTTPS must be used).

questions.questionHtml: Where does PowerShell store personalized aliases and functions so they persist across every new session?

options.html: They persist automatically with no configuration needed
In a PowerShell profile — a .ps1 script that runs at session start
Directly in the Windows registry, written automatically
In the $PSHOME environment variable

questions.explanationHtml: By default, aliases created interactively are lost when the session closes. To persist them, they need to be added to a PowerShell profile — a .ps1 script PowerShell checks for and runs automatically at session start.

options.html: Deletes the current profile
Creates the current user's PowerShell profile file, since none exists by default
Lists every profile path available to the host
Forces PowerShell to immediately reload its profile

questions.explanationHtml: Profiles don't exist by default — this command creates the "Current User, Current Host" profile file at the path stored in the $PROFILE automatic variable. -Force suppresses errors if intermediate folders are missing.

questions.questionHtml: Match each automatic variable to what it represents.
choices: The current object in the pipeline
The exit code of the last program run
The full path to the current user's profile
questions.explanationHtml: $_ is the pipelined object, $? reports TRUE/FALSE for the last operation's success, $LASTEXITCODE holds the exit code of the last Windows-based program run, and $PROFILE stores the current profile's path — all automatic variables PowerShell maintains itself.

questions.questionHtml: Match each command alias to the cmdlet it maps to.
questions.explanationHtml: PowerShell ships with familiar CMD/Unix-style aliases baked in: dir and ls both resolve to Get-ChildItem, type and cat resolve to Get-Content, gm to Get-Member, where to Where-Object, and kill to Stop-Process.
